claims.claim: T-27833 proposes closing the namespace-escape hole (a repo committer can create a Namespace resource matching the AppProject's clusterResourceWhitelist glob, e.g. `group1-project1-*`, and override the operator-set `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce` label to gain a privileged pod security boundary) by scoping namespace-kind permissions out of the impersonated sync service account while keeping Application bootstrapping on the control-plane SA. rfc-001-sync-impersonation.md only supports scoping `destinationServiceAccounts` per destination (server+namespace), not per resource kind within a sync, so as designed impersonation cannot separate 'create namespace during bootstrap' from 'apply namespace manifests during sync' for the same Application — the escape path T-27833 describes survives impersonation being enabled exactly as specced.

rfc-001-sync-impersonation.md's entire motivation is replacing a broad control-plane credential with narrow, per-destination impersonated service accounts so a compromised control plane no longer implies cluster-admin blast radius. T-28695 shows the Server-Side Diff reconcile path on external clusters ignores `destinationServiceAccounts` and instead authenticates as the raw cluster Secret credential, and because Kubernetes RBAC has no dry-run verb, every resource kind a chart introduces forces another standing `patch` grant onto that credential to keep diff working — the fleet has done this five times with no end state. This re-creates exactly the broad, always-write-capable control-plane credential rfc-001-sync-impersonation.md set out to eliminate, on any external cluster where diff is used.

rfc-001-sync-impersonation.md's open questions assert that Kubernetes audit trail events capture both the real and impersonated identity, making it possible to attribute sync actions to the correct per-Application/AppProject identity. T-28695 establishes that the Server-Side Diff path performs a write-authorized action (a dry-run `patch`) as the shared cluster credential rather than the impersonated SA on external clusters — so for that codepath the audit trail records only the generic control-plane identity, not the tenant whose Application triggered the request, breaking the per-tenant accountability rfc-001-sync-impersonation.md relies on to justify impersonation as a security control.

The same 'diff runs under a narrower/different identity than expected' failure mode is enforced inconsistently across two diff codepaths: T-26271 (root-caused in notes/note-1.md) shows the in-cluster CLI diff *does* run as the impersonated destination service account and fails when that SA lacks patch on cluster-scoped resources, while T-28695 shows the application-controller's Server-Side Diff on external clusters does the opposite — it ignores the impersonated SA entirely and runs as the standing cluster credential. Because enforcement of impersonation on the diff path depends on which component and cluster type is involved, an operator cannot reason about which identity actually computed a given diff, which is itself a gap in a control whose stated purpose is precise privilege attribution.

T-28239 places the hydrator's GPG signing key Secret in the same namespace as the rest of the Argo CD control plane, explicitly contradicting rfc-002-manifest-hydrator.md's stated need to keep git push credentials in a namespace separate from the rest of the components for extra protection. Reach: any Argo CD component or extension already scoped to read Secrets in that shared namespace (not just the commit server) can read the signing key. Gain: that reader can produce commits that pass SourceIntegrity verification on the hydrated branch — the same branch Argo CD treats as ground truth for what gets deployed — with no distinct check enforced at the point the key is consumed versus where it's stored, and no compensating control noted for that namespace-placement gap.

prd-progressive-sync-deletion.md's Reverse deletion strategy blocks step N+1 until the Application in step N is fully deleted. T-28511 shows that when one child Application in that sequence gets stuck in Progressing (e.g. a crashlooping resource) and is deleted outside the ApplicationSet's normal flow, the controller does not respect its Deleting status and restarts the wave from the top — so a user who only has delete access to that single child Application can drive the entire rollingSync group into a repeating delete/recreate loop, a blast radius far beyond the one Application they were authorized to act on.
